name: MCP6001T-I_OT
title: 1 MHz low-power rail-to-rail CMOS op amp: single, dual, quad
summary: A family of general-purpose CMOS operational amplifiers whose inputs and outputs both swing rail to rail, 1 MHz gain-bandwidth and about 100 µA supply current per amplifier, running from 1.8 V to 6.0 V. The MCP6001, MCP6001R and MCP6001U are singles in SC-70-5 or SOT-23-5 with three pin orders; the MCP6002 is a dual and the MCP6004 a quad. Inputs reach 0.3 V past both rails with picoamp bias current, and phase margin is 45° typical with a 500 pF load.
key_figures: within 25 mV of each rail (RL = 10 kΩ, 5.5 V)

circuits.title: Noninverting amplifier
circuits.description: A single amplifier gives a gain above one. The input drives VIN+ directly; R1 runs from the output back to VIN-, and R2 runs from VIN- to a reference voltage VREF. Gain from VIN to VOUT is 1 + R1/R2.

circuits.title: AC and DC test circuit
circuits.description: The bench used for most of the electrical figures. Two 100 kΩ / 100 kΩ resistor pairs make a difference amplifier with a gain of one: VP and VDD/2 set the non-inverting side, VM the inverting side, so VCM and VOUT can be set apart from each other. A 6.8 pF capacitor runs from the non-inverting node to ground and another across the inverting-side feedback resistor. The load is 10 kΩ (RL) returned to VL, in parallel with 60 pF (CL) to ground. VDD is bypassed by 100 nF and 1 µF.

circuits.title: Protecting the analog inputs
circuits.description: Input protection on both inputs of an amplifier with feedback resistor R3. R1 and R2 sit in series with the two inputs and cap the current drawn out of a pin when its source swings below VSS (the internal ESD diodes clamp there); each must exceed (VSS minus the lowest expected input) / 2 mA. D1 and D2, from each input pin to VDD, stop the pins rising far above VDD and pass that current into the VDD rail; R1 and R2 also limit their current. R3 is the feedback resistor from the output to VIN-.
notes: Diodes D1 and D2 may instead connect on the source side of R1 and R2; then something else must limit the diode current, and R1, R2 only limit inrush.

circuits.title: Output resistor for large capacitive loads
circuits.description: A unity-gain buffer driving a capacitive load CL through a series resistor RISO. Feedback is taken from the amplifier's own output pin, ahead of RISO, so the load looks resistive to the loop at high frequency and phase margin is kept. The RISO against CL/GN graph gives a starting value.

circuits.title: Unused op amp, circuit A (buffered reference)
circuits.description: One spare section of an MCP6004 wired as a follower of a divider: R1 and R2 split VDD and the amplifier buffers the result, VREF = VDD × R2 / (R1 + R2). The section sits at its lowest noise gain and its output does not toggle; VREF may be any level within the output range and can be used elsewhere.

circuits.title: Unused op amp, circuit B (fewest parts)
circuits.description: One spare section of an MCP6004 with VIN+ tied to VDD and VIN- tied to VSS, so it acts as a comparator held at a fixed state; no extra parts, though its supply current can be higher than circuit A's.

circuits.title: Instrumentation amplifier with unity-gain buffer inputs
circuits.description: Both halves of an MCP6002 buffer the two inputs, so the sources see the very high input impedance of the amplifiers. An MCP6001 then forms a difference amplifier with R1 = 20 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ: VOUT = (VIN2 – VIN1) × R1/R2 + VREF, a gain of 2 about the reference VREF.
notes: R1A, R1B are the two R1 positions (20 kΩ) and R2A, R2B the two R2 positions (10 kΩ).

circuits.title: Active second-order low-pass filter
circuits.description: A unity-gain Sallen-Key low-pass with a Butterworth response and a 100 kHz cutoff, values chosen with FilterLab. VIN passes through 14.3 kΩ and 53.6 kΩ in series to VIN+; 33 pF goes from VIN+ to ground and 100 pF from the junction of the resistors to the output, which also drives VIN-. The amplifier's 1 MHz bandwidth is only ten times the cutoff, so the response leans more on part tolerances than a design with a hundredfold margin.

circuits.title: Peak detector with clear and sample CMOS analog switches
circuits.description: Op amp A (half an MCP6002) with D1 inside its loop charges C1 through RISO to the highest VIN seen; feedback is taken from the diode's cathode. When VIN falls below the stored level D1 turns off and A swings to its rail. Op amp B (the other half) buffers VC1. A clock drives two CMOS switches: the sample switch first copies B's output through a second RISO onto C2 for tSAMP; then the clear switch connects R1 across C1 to ground for tCLEAR, discharging it with τ = R1·C1. Op amp C (an MCP6001) buffers VC2 to VOUT. C1's charging rate is set by A's short-circuit current: 25 mA into 0.1 µF gives 250 mV/µs, below the 0.6 V/µs slew rate; the capacitors are kept below 40 µF and RISO is picked as for any capacitive load.
notes: Timing per clock period: the sample signal pulses high for tSAMP on the rising clock edge, the clear signal then pulses high for tCLEAR, and the remainder until the next sample, tDETECT, is the detection window.

operation.text: MCP6001 (single, SC-70-5 or SOT-23-5), MCP6001R and MCP6001U (single, SOT-23-5 with other pin orders), MCP6002 (dual) and MCP6004 (quad) share one set of specifications. Each comes in an industrial grade (-40 °C to +85 °C) and an extended grade (-40 °C to +125 °C).
VDD sits 1.8 V to 6.0 V above VSS and the other pins stay between the two rails in normal use. The usual connection is a single positive supply with VSS at ground.

Put a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF capacitor on the supply pin (VDD in single-supply use) no more than 2 mm from it, and a bulk capacitor of 1 µF or more within 100 mm; neighbouring analog parts can use the same bulk capacitor.

Both inputs are CMOS gates: very high impedance, picoamp bias current. Two differential input pairs run in parallel, one for low and one for high common-mode voltage, which lets VCM go 0.3 V past either rail. The hand-over between them happens near VCM = VDD – 1.1 V; for lowest distortion and best gain linearity in noninverting stages keep the input away from that level.
The output does not reverse phase when an input goes beyond a supply rail.

ESD diodes at each input conduct when the pin is driven about one diode drop below VSS; above VDD a clamp breaks down at a level high enough for normal use and low enough to catch fast ESD events. The circuit around the part must keep each input within the absolute maximum voltage and ±2 mA current. With VCM under VSS the inputs source a large current (see the input current graph), so high-impedance circuits may need a narrower input range.
Each output behaves as a voltage source of low impedance. With RL = 10 kΩ to VDD/2 and VDD = 5.5 V the output reaches within 25 mV of each rail.

Phase margin is 90° typical and about 45° with 500 pF load. Rising load capacitance cuts phase margin and closed-loop bandwidth, showing as peaking and ringing; a unity-gain follower suffers most, though every gain behaves alike. Above roughly 100 pF at G = +1, add a series output resistor RISO with feedback taken ahead of it, start from the RISO graph using CL/GN, then confirm peaking and overshoot on the bench or in the SPICE model; bandwidth is lower than unloaded.

A spare section of the MCP6004 should not be left floating, so its output does not toggle and couple into its neighbours: wire it as a buffer of a divider (circuit A) or with VIN+ at VDD and VIN- at VSS (circuit B, fewer parts, may draw more current).

Board surface leakage between adjacent traces is about 10¹² Ω in dry air, so 5 V across it drives 5 pA, more than the 1 pA typical bias current at +25 °C. Surrounding the sensitive pins with a guard ring driven to their own potential reduces it. Noninverting stages and followers: guard ring to VIN-, which sits at the common-mode level, and the signal reaches VIN+ through a lead held off the board surface. Inverting and transimpedance stages (photodiode amplifiers among them): guard ring to VIN+, which sits at the reference such as VDD/2 or ground, and the signal reaches VIN- through a lead held off the board surface.

Low bias current allows large resistors and small capacitors in active filters, at the cost of more resistor noise and more effect from stray capacitance. An amplifier bandwidth of 100 times the cutoff frequency or more is the usual target; 10 times works but leaves the response more sensitive to part tolerances.
The DFN's exposed pad is connected inside to VSS and must be joined to VSS on the board.
